templates.scenario: You get this email in your work inbox. It is signed "IT Help Desk."
templates.prompt: Tap the line that should concern you.

segments.whyFine: A greeting is ordinary and asks nothing of you.

segments.text: We are moving everyone's {system} accounts to new servers this weekend.
segments.whyFine: Announcing a planned system change is normal and asks nothing of you.

segments.text: You do not need to do anything for the move itself.
segments.whyFine: This line says no action is needed, so it asks for nothing.

segments.text: To keep your account active, reply to this email with your current password.
segments.why: Asking you to send a password by email is a common phishing tactic. Real IT staff can move an account without asking you to send your password.

segments.text: Thank you for helping us finish on schedule.
segments.whyFine: A closing thank-you is ordinary and asks nothing of you.

templates.principle: Never send passwords or other login details by email or message, even when the request seems to come from your own workplace.

review.notes: Password-by-email is widely recognized as unsafe regardless of workplace; no unstated policy needed. Only one line makes a request.

templates.scenario: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. You just emailed a file with {client.plural}' contact details to a coworker who has no reason to see it. The coworker is inside your organization. Your workplace policy says any information sent to the wrong person must be reported to your {lead} as soon as it is noticed.[[twist]]

twists.text: It is late on a Friday afternoon.
Your {lead} looks busy with another task.

templates.prompt: What is the best next step?
templates.timing: Prompt reporting lets the right person contain the exposure; other containment steps are secondary and cannot replace the report.

options.text: Report the mistake to your {lead} right away, naming the file and who received it.
options.why: Prompt reporting lets the person responsible contain the problem and decide what else is needed. It is also what the workplace policy asks.

options.text: Resend the file to the right person so the work is not delayed, and carry on with your day.
options.why: Sending it correctly fixes the delivery but not the exposure. The wrong recipient still has the information, and the person responsible does not know.
options.misconception: Fixing the delivery fixes the problem.

options.text: Wait to see whether the coworker says anything before deciding whether it matters.
options.why: Waiting leaves client details exposed with no one managing the situation. The policy asks for a report when a mix-up is noticed, not when someone complains.
options.misconception: If no one complains, there was no harm.

options.text: Ask the coworker to delete the email without opening it, and mention it to your {lead} at the end of the day.
options.why: Asking for deletion is a reasonable step, but delaying the report means the person responsible cannot act while the problem is fresh, and the policy asks for a report as soon as it is noticed.
options.misconception: Quietly cleaning it up myself is enough, and the report can wait.

templates.principle: When information reaches the wrong person, report it right away through the proper channel; trying to fix it quietly or later takes the decision away from the people responsible.

review.notes: Internal misdirected email only; no legal notification duties asserted. Policy stated in scenario. Acceptable option is reasonable containment that delays the required report.

templates.scenario: The acceptable use policy at {workplace|the} says work computers are for work-related use only. During a slow period, {coworker} suggests streaming a movie on a work computer until things pick up.
templates.prompt: What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Decline politely, and use your own device during your break if you want to watch something.
options.why: The policy limits work computers to work use. Using your own device during a break respects the policy and gives you what you wanted.

options.text: Stream it quietly with the volume low, since no customers are around and it is a slow period.
options.why: A slow period does not change the policy. Personal streaming on work equipment is still outside what the policy allows.
options.misconception: If it is quiet, the rules relax.

options.text: Watch it only when your supervisor is out of sight, so that nobody has a reason to object.
options.why: Hiding the activity shows you know it is not allowed. The policy applies whether or not someone is watching.
options.misconception: The rule only applies when I am observed.

options.text: Log into your personal accounts on the work computer so the movie is on your own account.
options.why: Using personal logins on a work computer does not make the use work-related, and it can expose your accounts on a shared device.
options.misconception: My own account makes it my own use.

templates.principle: Use work devices only as your workplace's acceptable use policy allows, whether or not anyone is watching.

review.notes: Policy stated in scenario; no legal claims.

templates.scenario: You use your badge to open the staff entrance of {workplace|the}. A person you do not recognize follows right behind you without using a badge and says they forgot theirs. Your workplace rule is that everyone must badge in individually.

options.text: Politely stop them at the door and direct them to the front desk for a visitor or replacement badge.
options.why: The rule is that everyone badges in on their own. Pointing the person to the front desk follows it while staying courteous.

options.text: Hold the door and let them in, since they said they work here and it would be rude to refuse.
options.why: Politeness does not replace the rule. Someone who is not authorized could enter the building and reach people and information.
options.misconception: Being courteous means opening the door.

options.text: Ask for their name and then let them in if the name sounds familiar to you.
options.why: A name is easy to claim and does not verify identity. The front desk has the means to confirm who someone is.
options.misconception: Knowing a name is enough proof.

options.text: Say nothing and keep walking, assuming that someone further inside will deal with it.
options.why: Assuming someone else will handle it leaves an unverified person inside. You are at the door, so you are the first to act.

templates.principle: Follow badge and entry rules for everyone, politely; a person at the door is the first line of facility security.

review.notes: Workplace rule stated in the scenario.

templates.timing: The person is at the door right now, so action at the door comes first.

templates.scenario: Your workplace policy says {client|a}'s information must never be shared outside {workplace|the}. {coworker} posts a photo of the workspace on social media. Behind {coworker}, a screen showing {system|the} clearly displays {client|a}'s name and details.
templates.prompt: What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Tell {coworker} privately to take the photo down, and let your {lead} know what was visible.
options.why: Client information is visible to the public, which the policy forbids. Asking for removal limits exposure, and telling your {lead} lets them follow the proper steps.

options.text: Leave a public comment under the photo saying that it should be removed.
options.why: A public comment draws more attention to the photo and the exposed details. A private message is quicker and less visible.
options.misconception: Public correction is the fastest way to fix it.

options.text: Say nothing, since the details are small in the background and probably no one will read them.
options.why: The policy does not allow client information to be shared, even by accident. Small and unlikely to be noticed is not a safe standard.
options.misconception: If it is hard to see, it is not a problem.

options.text: Ask {coworker} to delete the photo, but do not mention it to anyone else to avoid getting {coworker} in trouble.
options.why: Removing the photo is a good step, but your {lead} needs to know client information was exposed so the right steps can be taken.
options.misconception: Protecting a coworker matters more than reporting.

templates.principle: Keep client information inside the workplace: ask for exposed details to be removed and tell the person responsible.

review.notes: Policy stated in scenario; no legal claims.

templates.scenario: You get this text message on your work phone.
templates.prompt: Tap the line that should concern you.
templates.docTitle: Text message to your work phone

segments.whyFine: Messages often start by naming who they are from. This line asks for nothing.

segments.text: We found a problem with your direct deposit.
segments.whyFine: Stating a reason for contact is normal and requests nothing yet.

segments.text: Click this link right now and enter your login to fix it today.
segments.why: Urgent pressure to click a link and enter your login is a common sign of a scam. Real requests do not need you to log in through a link in a message.

segments.text: Please call the number on your pay stub if you have questions.
segments.whyFine: Directing you to a number you already trust is a safe instruction.

templates.principle: Be wary of urgent messages that ask you to click a link and enter login details; verify through a channel you already trust.

review.notes: Single line applies pressure and requests credentials.

templates.scenario: At {workplace|the}, you click a link in an email and a page asks you to sign in. You realize it may be a scam. Your workplace's security procedure says IT must hear about suspected scams immediately.
templates.prompt: Put these actions in a sensible order.

steps.text: Stop and do not enter any information on the page
Write down what you clicked and when
Report it to IT right away
Follow IT's instructions, such as changing your password

precedence.why: Stopping first keeps the situation from getting worse before you report.
You stop interacting with the page before taking notes.
IT cannot give instructions until you have reported it.
Details noted help you give IT the facts before you act on instructions.

templates.principle: If you suspect a scam, stop, report to IT right away, and follow their instructions.

review.notes: Procedure stated in scenario; no specific technical or legal claims.
